lessons.title: WAI-ARIA Intro
lessons.interactiveContent:
Now that you know the basics of Accessibility, let's learn about accessibility standards.

WAI-ARIA stands for Web Accessibility Initiative-Accessible Rich Internet Applications and it's a specification for accessibility standards.

lessons.title: WAI-ARIA Importance
lessons.interactiveContent:
Meeting specific standards helps diverse users access content. As we saw, semantics is an important standard for accessibility.

However, sometimes we might not be able to use the HTML tags we wanted. Let's learn what to do in those cases!

lessons.title: Roles
lessons.interactiveContent:
Meaningful HTML tags like button or li help screen readers interpret content. But we'll find code that uses generic elements like div.

In these cases, we can improve accessibility with the role attributes. Add the attribute role with an empty value.

Make sure to pick role, followed by =, and finally "".

lessons.title: Role: banner
lessons.interactiveContent:
Role attributes provide meaning to the assistive technologies but don't change anything visually.

They help attach meaning to elements, like this "banner" role that tells the screen reader it is the header of the page.

Make sure to pick role, followed by banner.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Role attributes provide meaning to the assistive technologies but don't change anything visually.

They help attach meaning to elements, like this "banner" role that tells the screen reader it is the header of the page.

Complete the generic wrapper that introduces the Homeflix page as a banner.

Make sure to pick div, followed by role, and finally banner.

lessons.title: Roles: img
lessons.interactiveContent:
role also helps assistive technologies to identify blocks that need to be considered as a single block.

If we want screen readers to identify these images as a single image, we can assign the "img" role to the container.

Make sure to pick role, followed by =, and finally "img".

lessons.title: Roles: comment
lessons.interactiveContent:
The comment role implies a reaction to some content. Add this role to the div element to turn Chris' opinion into a comment.

Make sure to type comment.

lessons.title: Roles: contentinfo
lessons.interactiveContent:
The "contentinfo" role indicates that there's a footer at the end of the page. It contains copyright, contact, or privacy information.

Make sure to pick role, followed by =, and finally "contentinfo".
lessons.hardModeContent:
The "contentinfo" role indicates that there's a footer at the end of the page. It contains copyright, contact, or privacy information.

Treat the image group as one image, then give the copyright container its footer role.

Make sure to pick "img", followed by div, role, and finally "contentinfo".

lessons.title: Role: alert
lessons.interactiveContent:
Additionally, roles can provide further information. The "alert" role warns users about events or changes in content. Add it to the div element.

Make sure to pick role, followed by =, and finally "alert".
lessons.hardModeContent:
The "alert" role warns users about events or content changes.

Mark the session-expiry message as an alert on its div container.

Make sure to pick div, followed by role, and finally "alert".

lessons.title: Question: WAI-ARIA
lessons.interactiveContent:
What's the purpose of WAI-ARIA?

To ensure websites meet accessibility standardsTo use semantic tags

To ensure websites meet accessibility standards.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A page uses generic containers where semantic elements are unavailable. What does WAI-ARIA add for assistive technologies?

Extra meaning that assistive technologies can interpretA visual style that makes every element semanticA replacement for all native HTML elements

Extra meaning that assistive technologies can interpret.

lessons.title: Question: alert role
lessons.interactiveContent:
What changes can assistive technologies detect in an element with an alert role?

Changes in the contentChanges in the page structure

Changes in the content.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A message inside an element with the alert role changes from “Saving” to “Saved”. What change can assistive technologies detect?

The updated message contentOnly a change to the element's page positionOnly a change to the element's visual color

The updated message content.

lessons.title: Question: banner role
lessons.interactiveContent:
What kind of information do assistive technologies expect with this role?

Informative content located at the top of a page, similar to a <header>A normal paragraph

Informative content located at the top of a page, similar to a <header>.
lessons.hardModeContent:
The banner role identifies the page header for assistive technologies.

You replace banner with contentinfo. What meaning would the wrapper then communicate?

Page footer information, despite still containing the brand image and title.Page header information, because the h1 overrides the role.Navigation links, because every role describes navigation.

Page footer information, despite still containing the brand image and title.

lessons.title: Question: img role
lessons.interactiveContent:
What role would you use to help screen readers consider different images a single element?

The img roleThe images role

The img role.
lessons.hardModeContent:
A container combines several image files into one meaningful illustration. Which role should describe the container to a screen reader?

imgpresentationgroup

Make sure to pick img.

lessons.title: Question: Roles
lessons.interactiveContent:
When should we use the role attribute?

Only when we cannot use the semantic HTML tagWhenever we want

Only when we cannot use the semantic HTML tag.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Which situation calls for adding a role attribute?

You must keep a generic div but need to communicate the content meaning.You can use a native button that already communicates its purpose.You want to change a native heading font color.

You must keep a generic div but need to communicate the content meaning.

lessons.title: Question: contentinfo role
lessons.interactiveContent:
What kind of information can we see in a "contentinfo" role?

Copyright, contact, or privacy infoComments and reactions

Copyright, contact, or privacy info.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Which item belongs in a page area marked role="contentinfo"?

A link to the site's privacy policyThe page's main article headlineA product's add-to-cart button

A link to the site's privacy policy.

lessons.title: Example: alert role
lessons.interactiveContent:
Attach an alert role to the container to help screen readers identify this urgent information.

Make sure to pick role, followed by =, and finally "alert".
lessons.hardModeContent:
Attach an alert role to the container to help screen readers identify this urgent information.

Give the urgent discount its alert role and the copyright text its footer role.

Make sure to pick div, followed by role, "alert", and finally "contentinfo".

lessons.title: Example: banner role
lessons.interactiveContent:
Code a "banner" role to have the img and the h1 elements as the header of the page.

Make sure to type banner.

lessons.title: Example: comment role
lessons.interactiveContent:
This page provides reviews of movies. Include the "comment" role to help identify the review as a comment.

Make sure to pick role, followed by =, and finally "comment".
lessons.hardModeContent:
This page provides reviews of movies. Include the "comment" role to help identify the review as a comment.

Complete the wrapper that identifies Nina Taylor's review as a comment.

Make sure to pick div, followed by role, and finally "comment".

lessons.title: Example: contentinfo role
lessons.interactiveContent:
Add the contentinfo role to this element so that it provides meaning as a footer would do.

Make sure to type contentinfo.

lessons.title: Intro: other ARIA tools
lessons.interactiveContent:
You just learned why it's important to use the appropriate HTML tags or, if we can't use them, the appropriate ARIA roles.

Let's learn about one more attribute and how to use ARIA attributes correctly.

lessons.title: ARIA attribute: aria-hidden
lessons.interactiveContent:
Sometimes, we include visually attractive content that might distract screen readers. In these cases, we can use the aria-hidden attribute.

It'll hide content to assistive technologies, but it will still be visible on the page.

Make sure to pick aria-hidden.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Sometimes, we include visually attractive content that might distract screen readers. In these cases, we can use the aria-hidden attribute.

It'll hide content to assistive technologies, but it will still be visible on the page.

Keep this paragraph visible, but explicitly hide its message from screen readers.

Make sure to pick p, followed by aria-hidden, and finally "true".

lessons.title: ARIA attribute: aria-hidden
lessons.interactiveContent:
When screen readers go over elements with the attribute aria-hidden, they won't read their content to the user.

We must not use aria-hidden in interactive elements, such as
buttons or links, because users won't be able to interact with them.

Make sure to pick aria-hidden.
lessons.hardModeContent:
When screen readers go over elements with the attribute aria-hidden, they won't read their content to the user.

We must not use aria-hidden in interactive elements, such as
buttons or links, because users won't be able to interact with them.

Mark the decorative carousel container as hidden from screen readers without hiding it visually.

Make sure to pick div, followed by aria-hidden, and finally "true".

lessons.title: Bad ARIA
lessons.interactiveContent:
We need to ensure we are using ARIA roles when we need them.

For instance, this "banner" role is interfering with the real purpose of the ul, which is to show a list. So we shouldn't code it here.

lessons.title: Redundant Roles
lessons.interactiveContent:
When we code the semantic tag for an element, we do not need the role attribute. What's wrong with this code?

We do not need the role attribute in a button elementWe do not need the button tag in a button element

We do not need the role attribute in a button element.
lessons.hardModeContent:
When we use a semantic element, we do not need a matching role attribute.

Which change keeps the “Shop now” control semantically correct with the least code?

Remove role="button" and keep the button elementReplace the button element with a divKeep the role and remove the button's text

Remove role="button" and keep the button element.

lessons.title: Example: Using semantic tags
lessons.interactiveContent:
Always choose semantic tags over roles, they contain full accessibility support. Let's add a button element with the text "Click this button".

Make sure to pick button, followed by button.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Use semantic tags over roles because they have built-in accessibility support.

Create a native action control, not a link. Use the label Click this button.

Make sure to pick button, followed by Click this button, and finally button.

lessons.title: Question: aria-hidden
lessons.interactiveContent:
Does the aria-hidden attribute hide something visually in the element where it is used?

No, it doesn't visually hide anything. It hides content from assistive technologiesYes, the element doesn't appear anymore

No, it doesn't visually hide anything. It hides content from assistive technologies.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Use aria-hidden="true" to hide decorative content from assistive technologies while leaving it visible.

You remove that attribute from a decorative icon. What changes?

It stays visible and is no longer hidden from screen readers by that attribute.It disappears visually but becomes available to screen readers.It stays hidden from screen readers because the attribute used to be present.

It stays visible and is no longer hidden from screen readers by that attribute.

lessons.title: Question: Bad Aria
lessons.interactiveContent:
What is wrong with this code?

The role of the list shouldn't be "contentinfo"The li element shouldn't be inside the ul element

The role of the list shouldn't be "contentinfo".
lessons.hardModeContent:
The list contains navigation choices, not page-footer information. Which edit best fixes the accessibility issue?

Remove role="contentinfo" from the ulReplace each li with a divMove the links outside of the ul

Remove role="contentinfo" from the ul.

lessons.title: Example: aria-hidden
lessons.interactiveContent:
Can you hide the optional middle name to the screen reading here?

Make sure to pick aria-hidden.
lessons.hardModeContent:
Keep every form field accessible. Hide only the repeated optional note from screen readers while keeping it visible.

Make sure to pick div, followed by aria-hidden, and finally "true".
